title: Financial Power and Resource Command
question: Who controls the resources?
abstract: Every governance system must settle conflicting claims on finite resources. This paper treats that settlement as the financial pillar of a six-function model of governance and asks who controls resources across regime types. From a scarcity axiom and an explicit assumption that unsettled conflicts carry a positive hazard of dissolution, we prove that a collective with no recognized allocation regularity cannot persist with probability bounded away from zero, and that in any collective that does persist the share of conflicts settled by such a regularity tends to one. The result concerns a function, not an institution: in foraging bands the regularity is a sharing norm, and control is dispersed close to the minimum concentration the index allows. We then prove that the necessity of the pillar places no restriction on its concentration or contestability, show that aggregating subdomains understates concentration by exactly the cross-domain variance of control shares, and derive conditional comparative statics under which resource holders convert wealth into influence over rules. A comparison of market-capitalist societies, communist party-states, social democracies, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies and secular democracies finds the same function held by different institutions, with documented capture episodes and documented checks in every type. Seven hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claim testable. Revelation 13 and 18 are read typologically as images of economic participation conditioned on allegiance. The main limitation is that no coded cross-regime dataset yet exists, so the comparative claims remain qualitative.

title: Political Power and Rule Making
question: Who makes the laws?
abstract: Every governance system must settle who makes the rules. This paper treats rule making as one pillar of a six-function model of governance and separates two questions about it: whether the function is necessary, and how its control is distributed. From an axiom of plurality (members’ preferences diverge, yet some choices bind everyone), together with environmental change and the persistence of the group, we prove that every persistent collective implements a rule-making function, though not any particular institution. In stateless and consensus societies the function appears as camp discussion, lineage moots, oratory without command, and fission. We measure the distribution of rule-making power with power indices over decision procedures and prove that necessity places no constraint on concentration: for a group of n members and every k from 1 to n, some procedure satisfies the necessity lemma with concentration exactly 1/k. Three conditional propositions describe how rule making can turn into capture: monitoring incentives that vanish as organizations grow, veto structures that protect preferential status quo rules, and appointment channels that couple rule making to courts, security services, and the economy. We compare market capitalism, communist party-states, social democracy, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies, and secular democracies on identical questions, state seven hypotheses with falsifiers, and read Revelation 13 and 17 typologically as an image of rule-making authority that admits no contest. The main limitation is that no regime is coded numerically; the comparative claims are qualitative and await preregistered measurement.

title: Judicial Power and Legal Interpretation
question: Who interprets the laws?
abstract: Every governance system must decide who interprets its laws. General rules cannot settle particular disputes by themselves, because every rule admits more than one reasonable reading at its edges. This paper derives the judicial function from that fact. Under three explicit assumptions (open texture produces disputes that the parties cannot settle alone, self-help is costly to the collective, and exit is costly), any collective that persists indefinitely resolves all but finitely many such disputes through a determination procedure that neither party controls. The derivation requires a function, not an office. Leopard-skin chiefs, Barotse moots, Ju/’hoansi talking-out, qadi courts, the Parlement of Paris and modern constitutional courts all perform it. Two results narrow the claim. When exit is costless the forcing argument fails, which matches the thin adjudication of immediate-return foragers. When rules are executed by code, interpretation relocates to the classification of inputs instead of disappearing. The paper then operationalizes judicial contestability as a chain of disclosure, access, independence and compliance by the powerful, and proves that the probability that a captured ruling persists depends on the product of these links. An additive index can therefore score a judiciary well while a single broken link leaves capture unchecked. A comparison of six regime types, from market capitalism to historical Catholic monarchies, finds the function everywhere and finds wide variation in its concentration and coupling to other pillars. Eight hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claims testable. No numerical concentration scores are reported for real cases.

title: Ideological Power and Legitimation
question: Who shapes the beliefs?
abstract: Every governance system must settle who shapes the beliefs on which cooperation depends. This paper treats that question as the ideological pillar of a six-pillar model of governance and asks two things of it: whether the pillar is necessary, and when it becomes an instrument of capture. From a coordination axiom, together with membership turnover and the cross-cultural variability of rules, we derive that every persistent collective implements a recognition function: a recurring public practice that makes the operative rules common knowledge. The derivation establishes the necessity of a function, not of any institution, and it does not establish that belief in the rightness of rules is necessary. Stateless and egalitarian societies implement the function through talk, ridicule, ritual and kinship idiom, without a designated office. A Bayesian endorsement model then shows that a captured authority’s endorsement carries no information, that independent authorities raise expected public confidence in sound rules and lower it for unsound ones, and that coordinated control of several authorities lowers the probability that an error is disclosed below the level reached by independent control with the same average independence. We compare how academia, religious institutions, media, schools and medical and scientific bodies hold the function in market-capitalist, communist party-state, social-democratic, Islamic, Catholic-monarchical and secular-democratic regimes, and we state hypotheses with falsifiers. The comparative codings are qualitative and drawn from the historical and scholarly record, and each states what a quantitative estimate of concentration and integration would test.

title: Coercive Power and Enforcement
question: Who enforces the rules?
abstract: Every governance system must decide who enforces its rules. This paper derives the coercive function from one axiom, that members sometimes have reason to break rules, and compares how six regime types distribute it. A deterrence theorem shows that when the share of agents tempted to violate a rule exceeds the violation rate the collective can tolerate, compliance requires that violators’ continuation payoffs fall because of their own conduct. A sanction regime of some kind is therefore necessary, but no particular institution is. Gossip, ostracism and coalition action against would-be dominants meet this requirement as well as police do, as the ethnography of the Nuer, the Ju/’hoansi, Amazonian societies and Ostrom’s commons documents. A second result shows why, where sanctions are costly public goods and higher-order sanctions are absent, coercion at scale depends on provisioning or on shared norms of punishment. The paper then separates two properties of any enforcement apparatus: its conduct margin, how much more likely a violator is to be sanctioned than a complier, and its allegiance margin, how much more likely an opponent is to be sanctioned than a supporter. The two margins vary independently, so the necessity of coercion does not imply its capture. When capacity is limited, allegiance targeting weakens deterrence for at least one group; when opponents are targeted regardless of conduct, it also raises the volume of coercion against them, so spending and arrest counts mismeasure coercive power. The regime evidence is qualitative, and the paper specifies how both margins can be measured.

title: Productive Power and Social Reproduction
question: Who produces the wealth?
abstract: Every governance system consumes resources that someone must produce. This paper treats production, payment and social reproduction as the sixth pillar of a comparative framework in which six functions (resource allocation, rule-making, adjudication, legitimation, sanction and production) are present in every functioning polity. From a maintenance axiom we prove that a persistent collective must produce at a positive average rate and must reproduce its producers through care labor, and that rents, tribute, migration or automation relocate production rather than remove it. The same dependence gives producers a latent veto: when outside revenue falls short of the institutions’ maintenance requirement, a collective withdrawal of labor, taxes or trade threatens their persistence. A bargaining model makes the channels exact. Producers’ terms rise with their outside option and organized bargaining weight, fall linearly with the concentration of control over productive participation, and lose their withdrawal premium once rents cover the maintenance requirement. Restricting mobility pays only when the value of free exit exceeds the cost of enforcement, a condition that nests Domar’s land-labor hypothesis and Brenner’s emphasis on class organization. Every instrument that depresses producers’ terms is held in another pillar, so the capture of production never originates inside it. A comparison of six regime types finds the function everywhere and its capture only under specific couplings. Read typologically, Revelation 13:16 and 17 depict the limiting case in which exchange is conditioned on allegiance. The parameters are not estimated here; nine hypotheses state what would falsify the model.

title: The Formalized State
subtitle: The Hierarchy of the Beast System
question: What structure do all six functions share?
abstract: The six-pillar framework identifies an invariant structure of human governance, supported by historical observation and given precise expression through mathematics. Every governance system decides who controls resources, makes and interprets rules, shapes beliefs, enforces and produces. This paper defines the Formalized State, a class of structures with six layers of control, a role map and a dependency hypergraph, and proves four results relative to stated axioms and a stated set of preserved properties: roles, control shares, concentration, contestability, integration and dependencies. Representation: every governance system satisfying the axioms is equivalent to a Formalized State structure; content, ideology and procedure are forgotten. Necessity: six axioms about collective life (scarcity, plurality, generality, coordination, defection and maintenance) force the six functions, each axiom can fail in a persistent model, and four incidence axioms with falsifiers make the functions fully interdependent, although interpretation needs legitimation or coercion rather than both. Minimality: dropping or merging any pillar identifies systems that differ in a preserved property, with explicit witness pairs. Uniqueness: the abstraction is the coarsest one preserving those properties, unique up to unique isomorphism, with exactly six dimensions. Encodings of Aristotle, Weber, Parsons, Easton, Almond, Luhmann and Mann each identify two systems the abstraction distinguishes, so none is equivalent to it. Capture is a property of instances: structures satisfying every axiom occupy all four corners of the concentration and integration square. The regime analyses rest on the historical and ethnographic record, and the indices are defined so that real polities can be scored quantitatively.
